title: The first pledge of Aqaba
hook: twelve pledge not to steal, lie, kill their children or slander

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yathrib. Your line was: six listened. Did a stranger get your full attention, even for a minute? Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

A year goes by. The pilgrimage comes round again, and so do the men from Yathrib. This time, Ibn Ishaq says, there are twelve of them. They meet the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at the same spot, Aqaba, a narrow pass on the edge of Mina, away from the crowds. They've had a year at home to talk, to argue, to wonder. Now they've come back with their hands out. Not to ask for anything. To give their word. Today: the first pledge of Aqaba.
screen: `A YEAR LATER.` → `TWELVE COME BACK.` → `HANDS OUT TO PLEDGE.`

segments.voice: What did they promise? Ubada ibn al-Samit, whom the sirah names among the twelve, gives the terms in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet said: pledge to me that you will not set up any partner with God, that you will not steal, that you will not commit adultery, that you will not kill your children, that you will not bring a slander you have invented between your hands and feet, and that you will not disobey me in what is right. Whoever keeps it, his reward is with God. Look at that list. There's no army in it. No money. No promise to fight for anyone. It's almost entirely about how they will live. Their hands, their tongues, their homes, their children. Ibn Ishaq says this kind of pledge came to be called the pledge of women, and that it carried no promise of war. The Qur'an, in surah sixty, describes believing women pledging much the same things to the Prophet. And there's a mercy built in. In Ubada's report the Prophet adds: whoever falls into any of these and is punished in this world, that is an expiation. And whoever falls and God covers it, it is up to God, to forgive or to punish. So the pledge is clear, and it's also realistic. It expects people to be tested. It doesn't throw them away when they stumble. These twelve go home carrying a promise about conduct. Not yet a promise of protection. That comes later.
screen: `NO PARTNER WITH GOD.` · `NO STEALING, NO SLANDER.` · `NO ARMY, NO MONEY.` · `ROOM FOR THOSE WHO STUMBLE.` · then, large: `A PLEDGE OF CONDUCT.`

segments.voice: The practice: make one clear promise. Settle, and breathe. The twelve didn't promise to be good in general. They named things. So name one. Look over the list from the story: don't take what isn't yours, don't say what isn't true about someone, guard the people in your house. Or find your own. One behavior you know needs a line drawn under it. Say it to yourself in a single plain sentence, the kind you could actually keep. Not forever. Just clearly. Then sit with it. Notice whether it feels heavy, or light, or both. If you pray, you can place it before God. The bell holds the time.
Aqaba, the narrow pass where twelve men of Yathrib pledged the Prophet a way of living, not a war. Today's word.
Your line: a pledge of conduct. Today, keep the one plain promise you made in the sit, and notice the moment it gets tested. Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the first pledge of Aqaba as a promise about how to live, and the same list of conduct appears in the Qur'an's description of women pledging to the Prophet.

original.note: Arabic: a pledge of allegiance, given hand in hand.

trapdoor: what you thought: a loyalty oath to a leader.
what it means: twelve people promised a way of living, with room left for those who would stumble.
what a scholar hears: Ubada ibn al-Samit's report in Sahih al-Bukhari; Ibn Ishaq's note that it was later called the pledge of women, after the pledge described in the Qur'an (60:12).

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 18 (Ubada ibn al-Samit: the terms of the pledge; punishment in this world as expiation; if God covers it, it is up to Him)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (twelve men at Aqaba the following year; the 'pledge of women', with no obligation to fight)
Qur'an 60:12 (the pledge of the believing women)

notes: Count of twelve and 'a year later' are from Ibn Ishaq; confirm.
Bukhari 18 cited for Ubada's report; some readers link Bukhari 18 to the first Aqaba pledge, others to a later pledge. Confirm the attribution and number.
Terms paraphrased from Ubada's report; index hook says 'lie', the report says slander; written to the report.
Aqaba described as 'a narrow pass on the edge of Mina'; confirm.

Editor pass: Ubada is now 'named among the twelve in the sirah' rather than flatly 'one of the twelve' telling it, since Bukhari 18's link to the first Aqaba is debated; the 'pledge of women' line no longer states a reason Ibn Ishaq does not give, and the Qur'an 60:12 parallel is put as a separate, softer sentence.
Audit pass: checked against Bukhari 18 and Ibn Ishaq's pledge-of-women line; no change.
